System description:
# Case: Tesla Model S with Autopilot (Williston, Florida, 2016)

Source: NTSB Highway Accident Report HAR-17/02. This is a description of the system and its use before the crash. It does not include the investigation findings.

## System
A 2015 Tesla Model S has Autopilot, a SAE Level 2 partial driving automation feature. It combines Traffic-Aware Cruise Control (TACC) and Autosteer (lane keeping). The driver stays responsible for driving and monitoring the road.

## Main parts
- Sensors: a forward-facing camera, a forward-facing radar and ultrasonic sensors.
- Vision processing: a camera-based system detects lane markings and objects ahead.
- TACC: holds a speed set by the driver, slows down for a vehicle ahead in the same lane, and speeds up again when the lane is clear.
- Autosteer: keeps the vehicle centered in its lane using lane markings and the vehicle ahead.
- Forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking are available as separate features.
- Driver monitoring: the system checks that the driver's hands are on the steering wheel by sensing steering torque, and shows visual and audible alerts if no hands are detected for a period of time.

## People
- The driver sets the cruising speed, turns Autopilot on, and is told to keep hands on the wheel and watch the road.
- Other road users include cars, large trucks crossing or joining the road, and motorcyclists.

## Operating context
Autopilot is intended mainly for highways with limited access, in good visibility. Drivers can also turn it on for other roads, such as divided highways with cross traffic at intersections.

goals.text: Keep hands on the steering wheel.

Slow down for a vehicle ahead in the same lane.
Speed up again when the lane is clear.
Keep the vehicle centered in its lane.
Detect whether the driver's hands are on the steering wheel using steering torque.
Show visual and audible alerts when hands are not detected for a period of time.

requirements.text: The system shall detect a vehicle whose predicted path intersects the ego vehicle’s path, including a crossing or joining vehicle not classified as a same-lane lead vehicle, and shall reduce speed or brake when needed to avoid a collision.

When an object’s estimated trajectory creates a collision risk, the system shall issue a warning or apply braking even if the object’s detection confidence is low or it is classified as outside the relevant path.

While Autopilot is active, the system shall detect sustained driver inattention and issue an alert early enough for the driver to resume monitoring and intervene before a developing hazard requires a response.

The perception system shall represent a detected road user as a hazard candidate when its observed motion may cross the vehicle’s path, including when the road user’s orientation or classification is uncertain.

Before Autopilot activation and while it is active, the system shall clearly inform the driver that Autopilot does not assume responsibility for driving or hazard monitoring and that the driver must remain ready to steer or brake.
The system shall warn the driver and inhibit Autopilot activation when the detected road context includes cross traffic for which Autopilot is not intended.
The system shall not treat steering torque alone as proof that the driver’s hands are on the wheel; when hand presence cannot be verified, it shall treat hand status as unknown.

The system shall alert the driver when monitoring indicates inattention, regardless of whether steering torque is detected, and shall issue a hands-off alert promptly when hand presence is not verified.

While Autopilot is active, the system shall detect when required camera or radar data is unavailable, blocked, or stale, alert the driver, and suspend the affected automated control until usable data is restored.

Before increasing speed, TACC shall assess whether any detected or uncertain object may make the vehicle’s path unsafe, including crossing or joining traffic, and shall withhold acceleration when such a hazard is present.
